decks.title: Introduction to Trigonometry — Part 1: Ratios and standard angles
goals: Define the six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle of a right triangle
Explain why the ratios depend only on the angle
Find all the ratios when one is given
Evaluate expressions and find angles using these values

slides.heading: Introduction to Trigonometry, Part 1: Ratios of an angle
slides.body_md: Trigonometry compares the sides of a right triangle, as seen from one of its acute angles.

visual.alt: Right triangle ABC with the right angle at B and the angle theta marked at A; the side next to theta is labelled adjacent, the side across from theta is labelled opposite, and the longest side is the hypotenuse.
visual.caption: Every ratio compares two sides, seen from the marked angle.

slides.narration: Welcome to trigonometry. The word means measuring triangles. Builders of ramps and roofs, surveyors and pilots all use it. Everything starts with a right triangle and one acute angle, which we call theta. From that angle, the three sides get names, and comparing them in pairs gives six numbers that belong to the angle itself.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Explain why they depend only on the angle
Find all six ratios from one
Evaluate expressions and find unknown angles
slides.narration: Here are your goals. One note on the syllabus: ratios of complementary angles are not part of your course this year, so we will not use them. You need the six definitions, the standard values, and in part two, the identities.

slides.heading: Naming the sides
slides.body_md: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, seen from $\angle A$: $BC$ is **opposite**, $AB$ is **adjacent**, and $AC$ is the **hypotenuse**.

visual.alt: Right triangle ABC, right-angled at B: AB is the side adjacent to angle A, BC is the side opposite angle A, and AC, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse.
visual.caption: Names of sides depend on which acute angle you stand at.

slides.narration: The hypotenuse is always the side across from the right angle, and it is the longest side. The other two names depend on where you stand. From angle A, the side across is the opposite side and the one touching A is the adjacent side. Stand at angle C instead, and those two names swap.

slides.heading: The six trigonometric ratios
slides.body_md: For the acute angle $A$:

visual.alt: Table of the six ratios: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, three fifths; cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, four fifths; tangent is opposite over adjacent, three quarters; cosecant, secant and cotangent are their reciprocals, five thirds, five quarters and four thirds.
visual.caption: The last three are reciprocals of the first three.

slides.narration: Sine A is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine A is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent A is opposite over adjacent. The other three are simply these fractions turned upside down: cosecant, secant and cotangent. In the three four five triangle, sine A is three fifths. Notice that sine A is one symbol, not sine times A.

slides.heading: Why the ratios depend only on the angle
slides.body_md: Two right triangles with the same acute angle $A$ are **similar** (AA), so their sides are proportional and every ratio is the same.

visual.alt: Two right triangles sharing the angle A: the small one has legs 4 and 3 and hypotenuse 5, the large one has legs 8 and 6 and hypotenuse 10. In both, the side opposite A divided by the hypotenuse is three fifths.
visual.caption: Same angle, similar triangles: $\sin A = \dfrac35 = \dfrac{6}{10}$ in both.

slides.narration: Here two right triangles share the angle A. The big one is the small one scaled up by two. Because the triangles are similar, the opposite side over the hypotenuse is three fifths in both. So sine A does not depend on the size of the triangle, only on the angle. That is why we can talk about the sine of an angle at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: all ratios from one
slides.body_md: If $\tan A = \dfrac{5}{12}$, find the other five ratios.

visual.alt: Right triangle with the angle A at the left: adjacent side 12 k, opposite side 5 k and hypotenuse 13 k, drawn to shape.
visual.caption: $\tan A = \dfrac{5}{12}$: the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{144 + 25}\,k = 13k$.

slides.narration: A ratio tells us the shape, not the size, so write the sides as five k and twelve k. Pythagoras gives the hypotenuse, thirteen k. Now every ratio can be read off, and the k cancels each time. A quick check: sine divided by cosine should give back the tangent you started with.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: ratios in a given triangle
slides.body_md: In triangle $PQR$, right-angled at $Q$, $PQ = 8$ cm and $PR = 17$ cm. Find $\sin P$, $\cos P$ and $\tan R$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** From $P$: opposite $QR = 15$, adjacent $PQ = 8$. So $\sin P = \dfrac{15}{17}$, $\cos P = \dfrac{8}{17}$.

visual.alt: Right triangle PQR, right-angled at Q, drawn to scale: PQ is 8 centimetres, the hypotenuse PR is 17 centimetres, and QR is unknown.
visual.caption: Find $QR$ first, by Pythagoras.

slides.narration: First find the missing side with Pythagoras. Then, for each ratio, stand at the angle named and say which side is opposite and which is adjacent. At P, the opposite side is fifteen. At R, the opposite side is eight. Mixing up the viewpoint is the most common error in this chapter.

slides.heading: Quick check: read a ratio
slides.body_md: Find the hypotenuse, then stand at angle $A$.
slides.narration: Use Pythagoras for the third side. Which side is across from angle A, and which is the hypotenuse?

slides.heading: Relations between the ratios
slides.body_md: The ratios are linked, so knowing one tells you the rest.

rows: divide opposite and adjacent by the hypotenuse
$\operatorname{cosec} A = \dfrac{1}{\sin A}$, $\sec A = \dfrac{1}{\cos A}$, $\cot A = \dfrac{1}{\tan A}$
the fractions are turned upside down
the hypotenuse is the longest side
$\tan A$ can be any positive number
either leg can be the longer one

visual.alt: Table of relations: tangent is sine over cosine; cosecant, secant and cotangent are reciprocals of sine, cosine and tangent; for an acute angle sine and cosine lie between 0 and 1 because the hypotenuse is longest; tangent can be any positive number.
visual.caption: Use these to move from one ratio to another.

slides.narration: Tangent is sine divided by cosine, because dividing opposite and adjacent by the same hypotenuse does not change their ratio. The reciprocals pair up. And since the hypotenuse is the longest side, sine and cosine of an acute angle are always between zero and one. Tangent has no such limit.

slides.heading: The ratios of 45°
slides.body_md: An isosceles right triangle has two $45^\circ$ angles and legs $a$, $a$, so its hypotenuse is $\sqrt2\,a$.

visual.alt: Isosceles right triangle with equal legs a and hypotenuse root 2 times a; both acute angles measure 45 degrees.
visual.caption: Equal legs: $\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.

slides.narration: Now we find exact values for special angles. In an isosceles right triangle the two legs are equal, so tangent forty five degrees is one. The hypotenuse is root two times a leg, so sine and cosine of forty five degrees are both one over root two.

slides.heading: The ratios of 30° and 60°
slides.body_md: Cut an equilateral triangle of side $2a$ in half: $BD = a$, $AD = \sqrt3\,a$.

visual.alt: Equilateral triangle ABC of side 2 a with the perpendicular AD to BC; D is the midpoint, BD is a, AD is root 3 times a, angle B is 60 degrees and angle BAD is 30 degrees.
visual.caption: Half an equilateral triangle gives both $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

slides.narration: All angles of an equilateral triangle are sixty degrees. The perpendicular from the top cuts it into two right triangles, each with angles of thirty and sixty degrees. With side two a, the short leg is a and Pythagoras gives the long leg as root three times a. Read the ratios from the shaded triangle.

slides.heading: Table of values
slides.body_md: Learn the sine row; the others follow. $\tan 90^\circ$, $\sec 90^\circ$, $\operatorname{cosec} 0^\circ$ and $\cot 0^\circ$ are not defined.

visual.alt: Table of trigonometric ratios at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: sine rises 0, one half, one over root 2, root 3 over 2, 1; cosine falls through the same values; tangent is 0, one over root 3, 1, root 3, and not defined at 90 degrees; the reciprocals follow.
visual.caption: Sine rises from $0$ to $1$; cosine falls from $1$ to $0$.

slides.narration: Here is the whole table. A memory trick: the sine row is root zero, root one, root two, root three and root four, each divided by two. Cosine is the same row backwards. Tangent is sine over cosine, so at ninety degrees it would need division by zero: it is not defined.

slides.heading: Quick check: use the table
slides.body_md: Square the values before you subtract.
slides.narration: Write each value from the table, square it, then multiply. Which term do you subtract?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: evaluate an expression
slides.body_md: Evaluate $4\sin^2 30^\circ + 3\tan^2 60^\circ - 2\cos^2 45^\circ$.

visual.alt: Working table: 4 sine squared 30 degrees is 1; 3 tangent squared 60 degrees is 9; 2 cosine squared 45 degrees is 1; so the expression is 1 plus 9 minus 1, which is 9.
visual.caption: Square the value, then multiply.

slides.narration: Write the three values first. Then square each, carefully: root three squared is three, and one over root two squared is one half. Finally multiply and add. Writing the values on a separate line earns a mark even if the arithmetic later slips.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: find the angles
slides.body_md: Find acute angles $A$ and $B$ ($A > B$) if $\sin(A - B) = \dfrac12$ and $\cos(A + B) = \dfrac12$.

visual.alt: Working table: sine of A minus B equal to one half gives A minus B equal to 30 degrees; cosine of A plus B equal to one half gives A plus B equal to 60 degrees; adding gives A equal to 45 degrees and subtracting gives B equal to 15 degrees.
visual.caption: Turn each ratio equation into an angle equation.

slides.narration: Read each equation backwards in the table: which angle has sine one half? Thirty degrees. Which has cosine one half? Sixty degrees. That gives two simple equations in A and B. Add and subtract them, and check by substituting the angles back.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: sides from an angle
slides.body_md: In triangle $PQR$, right-angled at $Q$, $QR = 9$ cm and $\angle P = 60^\circ$. Find $PQ$ and $PR$.

visual.alt: Right triangle PQR, right-angled at Q, with angle P equal to 60 degrees; QR, opposite P, is 9 centimetres; PQ and PR are unknown.
visual.caption: Opposite side known: use $\tan P$ for $PQ$ and $\sin P$ for $PR$.

slides.narration: Choose each ratio so that it links the side you know with the side you want. From P, nine centimetres is the opposite side. To get the adjacent side, use tangent. To get the hypotenuse, use sine. Rationalise the answers, and confirm with Pythagoras.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the angle
slides.body_md: Read the table backwards.
slides.narration: Rearrange to get tangent theta alone. Which standard angle has that tangent?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ratios depend only on the angle (similar triangles)
One ratio given: sides $k$, Pythagoras, then all ratios
Standard values from the $45^\circ$ and half-equilateral triangles

visual.alt: Table of trigonometric ratios at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: sine rises 0, one half, one over root 2, root 3 over 2, 1; cosine falls through the same values; tangent is 0, one over root 3, 1, root 3, and not defined at 90 degrees; the reciprocals follow.
visual.caption: Sine rises from $0$ to $1$; cosine falls from $1$ to $0$.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Name the sides from the angle, then take the ratios. They depend only on the angle, because similar triangles have proportional sides. From one ratio you can find all the others. And the special triangles give exact values that you should know by heart.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Ratios from one ratio (2 marks):** third side by Pythagoras 1 + ratios 1
**Evaluate (2–3 marks):** values written 1 + substitution 1 + simplified answer 1
**Find angles (2 marks):** angle equations 1 + both angles 1
**Mistake:** reading opposite and adjacent from the wrong angle
**Mistake:** using complementary-angle results (not in the 2026–27 syllabus)
slides.narration: Write the values from the table on their own line before substituting. Show the third side of the triangle with Pythagoras; it carries a mark. The classic slips are reading sides from the wrong angle and misreading squares of ratios. Stick to the methods in this syllabus.

decks.title: Introduction to Trigonometry — Part 2: Trigonometric identities
goals: Prove sin²A + cos²A = 1 from Pythagoras’ theorem
Derive 1 + tan²A = sec²A and cot²A + 1 = cosec²A
Find all ratios from one using identities
Prove simple identities step by step
Use identities to evaluate expressions under a condition

slides.heading: Introduction to Trigonometry, Part 2: Identities
slides.body_md: In a right triangle with hypotenuse $1$, the legs are $\cos A$ and $\sin A$.

visual.alt: Right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and acute angle A: the adjacent leg has length cosine A and the opposite leg has length sine A.
visual.caption: Hypotenuse $1$: the legs are $\cos A$ and $\sin A$, so $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Picture a right triangle whose hypotenuse is exactly one unit long. Its legs are then cosine A and sine A. Pythagoras says the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse. So sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, whatever the angle. Equations like this, true for every angle, are called identities.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use a given condition to evaluate an expression
slides.narration: These are your goals. Proving an identity is like solving a puzzle: you transform one side, step by step, until it matches the other. The proof of the first identity is itself a common five mark question, so learn it carefully.

slides.heading: Proving the first identity
slides.body_md: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$: $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$. Divide every term by $AC^2$:

visual.alt: Right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, with angle A marked; the legs AB and BC and the hypotenuse AC are labelled.
visual.caption: $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$ — divide by one side squared.

slides.narration: Start with Pythagoras. Divide every term by the hypotenuse squared. The first fraction is cosine A squared, the second is sine A squared, and the right side becomes one. That is the whole proof. It also holds at zero and ninety degrees, where you can check it with the table.

slides.heading: Three identities from one theorem
slides.body_md: Dividing $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$ by each side squared gives three identities.

visual.alt: Table of the three identities: sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1, from dividing by AC squared, for 0 to 90 degrees; 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared, from dividing by AB squared, for 0 up to but not including 90 degrees; cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared, from dividing by BC squared, for angles above 0 up to 90 degrees.
visual.caption: One theorem, three identities.

slides.narration: Divide by A B squared instead, and you get one plus tangent squared equals secant squared. Divide by B C squared, and you get cotangent squared plus one equals cosecant squared. Note the angle limits: tangent and secant are not defined at ninety degrees, and cotangent and cosecant are not defined at zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ratios using identities
slides.body_md: Given $\sec\theta = \dfrac{25}{7}$ ($\theta$ acute), find $\tan\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ without drawing a triangle.

visual.alt: Flow: from secant theta equal to 25 over 7, the identity gives tangent squared equal to 576 over 49, so tangent theta is 24 over 7; the reciprocal gives cosine theta equal to 7 over 25; multiplying tangent by cosine gives sine theta equal to 24 over 25.
visual.caption: Identities and reciprocals, no triangle needed.

slides.narration: Here the identity does the work of Pythagoras. Secant squared minus one gives tangent squared. Take the positive square root, because the angle is acute. A reciprocal gives cosine, and multiplying tangent by cosine gives sine. Always finish with the check that sine squared plus cosine squared is one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: simplify with identities
slides.body_md: Find the value of $\cos^2\theta(1 + \tan^2\theta) + \sin^2\theta(1 + \cot^2\theta)$.
bullets: **Step 3 —** The value is $1 + 1 = 2$, for every acute $\theta$.

visual.alt: Working table: the expression becomes cosine squared times secant squared plus sine squared times cosecant squared, which is 1 plus 1, which is 2.
visual.caption: Recognise $1 + \tan^2\theta$ and $1 + \cot^2\theta$ on sight.

slides.narration: Learn to spot the patterns one plus tangent squared and one plus cotangent squared. Each becomes a single reciprocal squared, which then cancels with the ratio in front. The answer does not depend on theta at all. A quick check at forty five degrees confirms it.

slides.heading: Quick check: use an identity
slides.body_md: Look for $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta$.
slides.narration: Take out the common factor. What does the bracket equal for every angle?

slides.heading: How to prove an identity
slides.body_md: Transform **one side** until it becomes the other. Never treat an identity as an equation to be solved.

nodes.label: Start from the more complicated side
Can an identity replace a bracket?
Factorise or use a common denominator
Multiply by a conjugate, e.g. $1 - \sin A$

visual.alt: Strategy chart for proving identities: start from the more complicated side; replace brackets using identities where possible, otherwise write everything in sine and cosine; factorise or combine fractions; if stuck, multiply by a conjugate such as 1 minus sine A; continue until you reach the other side exactly.
visual.caption: Work on one side only; never move terms across the equals sign.

slides.narration: Here is a strategy. Begin with the side that looks more complicated. If a bracket matches an identity, replace it. If not, rewrite everything in sine and cosine. Then combine fractions or factorise. If you get stuck with something like one plus sine A, multiplying by its conjugate often unlocks it. Write one reason for each step.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a difference of squares
slides.body_md: Prove that $\sin^4 A - \cos^4 A = 1 - 2\cos^2 A$.

visual.alt: Proof table: sine to the fourth A minus cosine to the fourth A factorises as a difference of squares; the second bracket is 1; and replacing sine squared A by 1 minus cosine squared A gives 1 minus 2 cosine squared A.
visual.caption: Each line carries its reason.

slides.narration: Fourth powers are squares of squares, so factorise as a difference of two squares. One bracket is the famous identity and becomes one. Then replace sine squared by one minus cosine squared. Three short steps, each with a reason, is exactly what examiners want to see.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: sine and cosine form
slides.body_md: Prove that $\tan A + \cot A = \sec A\operatorname{cosec} A$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** $= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A\cos A} = \dfrac{1}{\sin A\cos A}$.

rows: $\tan A + \cot A = \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}$

visual.alt: Proof table: tangent A plus cotangent A written in sine and cosine, combined over sine A cosine A, the numerator becomes 1, giving secant A times cosecant A.
visual.caption: Sine-and-cosine form, then the identity.

slides.narration: When no identity jumps out, rewrite in sine and cosine. Two fractions with different denominators combine over sine A times cosine A. The numerator is our identity, so it becomes one. Splitting the fraction into two reciprocals gives the right side.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: multiply by the conjugate
slides.body_md: Prove that $\dfrac{1 + \sin A}{\cos A} = \dfrac{\cos A}{1 - \sin A}$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Multiply the LHS above and below by $1 - \sin A$: $\dfrac{(1 + \sin A)(1 - \sin A)}{\cos A(1 - \sin A)}$.
**Step 3 —** $\dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\cos A(1 - \sin A)} = \dfrac{\cos A}{1 - \sin A} =$ RHS.
**Contrast —** Cross-multiplying both sides proves nothing unless you say that it is reversible; the conjugate method works on one side only.

visual.alt: Proof table: multiply one plus sine A over cosine A, top and bottom, by one minus sine A; the numerator becomes cosine squared A; cancelling one cosine A gives cosine A over one minus sine A.
visual.caption: The conjugate turns $1 + \sin A$ into $\cos^2 A$.

slides.narration: The right side has one minus sine A at the bottom, which suggests the conjugate. Multiplying top and bottom by one minus sine A does not change the value. The top becomes one minus sine squared, which is cosine squared, and one cosine cancels. This trick appears in many board questions.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Is it an identity?
slides.narration: Rearrange one of the three identities. Does this statement match it for every acute angle?

slides.heading: Worked example 6: using a condition
slides.body_md: If $5\sin\theta - 12\cos\theta = 0$ ($\theta$ acute), find $\sin\theta + \cos\theta$.

visual.alt: Right triangle with angle theta at the left: adjacent side 5 k, opposite side 12 k and hypotenuse 13 k.
visual.caption: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{12}{5}$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$.

slides.narration: A condition linking sine and cosine usually gives the tangent. From there, the secant identity gives cosine, and sine follows. The figure shows the triangle these values describe: legs five k and twelve k, hypotenuse thirteen k. Always substitute back into the condition to check.

slides.heading: Quick check: identity in action
slides.body_md: Find $\cos\theta$ first.
slides.narration: Use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one to find cosine. Then take its reciprocal.

slides.heading: Checking an identity with numbers
slides.body_md: Substituting standard angles is a quick test. Agreement at a few angles does **not** prove an identity, but disagreement at one angle disproves it.

visual.alt: Check table: at 30 degrees both sides are 4 over root 3; at 45 degrees both are 2; at 60 degrees both are 4 over root 3.
visual.caption: A numerical check catches slips — but it is not a proof.

slides.narration: Before or after a proof, it is wise to test the identity at a couple of standard angles. If the two sides disagree even once, the statement is not an identity, and you have caught an error. But agreeing at three angles is not a proof; only the algebra shows it holds for every angle.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ratios from one ratio: identity, reciprocal, product
Proofs: one side at a time; sine–cosine form; factorise; conjugate

visual.alt: Table of the three identities: sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1, from dividing by AC squared, for 0 to 90 degrees; 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared, from dividing by AB squared, for 0 up to but not including 90 degrees; cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared, from dividing by BC squared, for angles above 0 up to 90 degrees.
visual.caption: One theorem, three identities.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. One theorem, divided three ways, gives three identities. Use them to find ratios without triangles, to simplify expressions, and to prove new identities step by step. And remember: test with numbers, but prove with algebra.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Prove $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$ (3–5 marks):** figure and Pythagoras 1 + division 1 + conclusion 1 (+ derived identities with ranges)
**Prove an identity (2–3 marks):** each correct step with its reason 1
**Evaluate under a condition (2–3 marks):** ratio found 1 + identity used 1 + value 1
**Mistake:** working on both sides at once, or moving terms across
**Mistake:** dropping the condition "acute" when taking square roots
slides.narration: In identity proofs, examiners give marks step by step, so never skip a line and always name the identity you use. Start from one side and finish exactly at the other. Remember that a square root of a sum is not the sum of the square roots, and that for acute angles every ratio is positive.

notes.title: Introduction to Trigonometry — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Trigonometric ratios of an acute angle
sections.body_md:
In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, seen from the acute angle $A$: $BC$ is the side **opposite** $A$, $AB$ the side **adjacent** to $A$, and $AC$ the **hypotenuse**.

$$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}, \quad \cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}, \quad \tan A = \frac{BC}{AB},$$
$$\operatorname{cosec} A = \frac{1}{\sin A}, \quad \sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A}, \quad \cot A = \frac{1}{\tan A}, \quad \tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}.$$

$\sin A$ is one symbol (not "$\sin \times A$"); $\sin^2 A$ means $(\sin A)^2$. For an acute angle, $0 < \sin A < 1$ and $0 < \cos A < 1$ (the hypotenuse is the longest side), while $\tan A$ can be any positive number.

key_terms.definition_md: The side opposite the right angle; the longest side.
A ratio of two sides of a right triangle, seen from one acute angle.

visual.alt: Right triangle ABC, right-angled at B: AB is the side adjacent to angle A, BC is the side opposite angle A, and AC, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse.
visual.caption: Names of sides depend on which acute angle you stand at.

visuals.alt: Table of the six ratios: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, three fifths; cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, four fifths; tangent is opposite over adjacent, three quarters; cosecant, secant and cotangent are their reciprocals, five thirds, five quarters and four thirds.
visuals.caption: The last three are reciprocals of the first three.

sections.heading: 2. Why the ratios are well defined; one ratio gives all
sections.body_md:
Two right triangles with the same acute angle $A$ are similar (AA criterion), so corresponding sides are proportional and each ratio has the same value in both. The ratios depend **only on the angle**.

**One ratio given:** write two sides as multiples of $k$, find the third by Pythagoras, then read every ratio. Example: $\tan A = \dfrac{5}{12}$ gives sides $5k$, $12k$, $13k$, so $\sin A = \dfrac{5}{13}$, $\cos A = \dfrac{12}{13}$.

**Sides from a ratio:** a ratio fixes the shape only. $\sin A = \dfrac35$ allows opposite $3$ cm and hypotenuse $5$ cm, or $6$ cm and $10$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: Having one value for each angle, whatever the size of the triangle.

visual.alt: Two right triangles sharing the angle A: the small one has legs 4 and 3 and hypotenuse 5, the large one has legs 8 and 6 and hypotenuse 10. In both, the side opposite A divided by the hypotenuse is three fifths.
visual.caption: Same angle, similar triangles: $\sin A = \dfrac35 = \dfrac{6}{10}$ in both.

visuals.alt: Right triangle with the angle A at the left: adjacent side 12 k, opposite side 5 k and hypotenuse 13 k, drawn to shape.
visuals.caption: $\tan A = \dfrac{5}{12}$: the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{144 + 25}\,k = 13k$.

sections.heading: 3. Ratios of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
sections.body_md:
- **$45^\circ$:** an isosceles right triangle with legs $a$ has hypotenuse $\sqrt2\,a$: $\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.
- **$30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$:** half of an equilateral triangle of side $2a$ has legs $a$ and $\sqrt3\,a$: $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac12$, $\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac12$, $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$.
- **$0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$:** $\sin 0^\circ = 0$, $\cos 0^\circ = 1$, $\sin 90^\circ = 1$, $\cos 90^\circ = 0$; $\tan 90^\circ$, $\sec 90^\circ$, $\operatorname{cosec} 0^\circ$, $\cot 0^\circ$ are not defined.

As $A$ increases from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, $\sin A$ increases from $0$ to $1$ and $\cos A$ decreases from $1$ to $0$.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* trigonometric ratios of complementary angles.

key_terms.definition_md: $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, whose ratios are known exactly.

visual.alt: Table of trigonometric ratios at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees: sine rises 0, one half, one over root 2, root 3 over 2, 1; cosine falls through the same values; tangent is 0, one over root 3, 1, root 3, and not defined at 90 degrees; the reciprocals follow.

sections.heading: 4. Using the standard values
sections.body_md:
**Evaluating:** write each value, square or multiply as the expression says, then simplify. $4\sin^2 30^\circ + 3\tan^2 60^\circ - 2\cos^2 45^\circ = 1 + 9 - 1 = 9$.

**Finding angles:** read the table backwards. $\sqrt3\tan\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^\circ$. Two equations such as $\sin(A - B) = \dfrac12$, $\cos(A + B) = \dfrac12$ give $A - B = 30^\circ$, $A + B = 60^\circ$, so $A = 45^\circ$, $B = 15^\circ$.

**Sides of a triangle:** choose the ratio that links the known side and the wanted side. With $QR = 9$ cm opposite $\angle P = 60^\circ$: $PQ = \dfrac{9}{\tan 60^\circ} = 3\sqrt3$ cm and $PR = \dfrac{9}{\sin 60^\circ} = 6\sqrt3$ cm.

Sines do not add: $\sin 30^\circ + \sin 60^\circ \ne \sin 90^\circ$.

sections.heading: 5. The three identities
sections.body_md:
In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$. Dividing by $AC^2$, $AB^2$ and $BC^2$ in turn:

$$\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1 \quad (0^\circ \le A \le 90^\circ)$$
$$1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A \quad (0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ)$$
$$\cot^2 A + 1 = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A \quad (0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ)$$

An **identity** is true for every angle for which both sides are defined. With them, one ratio gives all the others without a triangle: $\sec\theta = \dfrac{25}{7}$ gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{24}{7}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{7}{25}$, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{24}{25}$.

key_terms.definition_md: An equation true for all values of the angle for which both sides are defined.

sections.heading: 6. Proving identities
sections.body_md:
Work on **one side** (usually the more complicated) until it becomes the other; never move terms across "=".

1. Replace a bracket by an identity when one matches: $1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A$, $1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A$.
2. Otherwise write everything in $\sin$ and $\cos$, then combine fractions.
3. Factorise: $\sin^4 A - \cos^4 A = (\sin^2 A - \cos^2 A)(\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A)$.
4. Multiply by a conjugate: $\dfrac{1 + \sin A}{\cos A} \times \dfrac{1 - \sin A}{1 - \sin A} = \dfrac{\cos A}{1 - \sin A}$.

**Conditions:** a relation like $5\sin\theta = 12\cos\theta$ gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{12}{5}$, then the identities give the rest. **Squaring sums:** $(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, so $\sin\theta + \cos\theta \le \sqrt2$.

Test with $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$ to catch errors — but numbers never replace the proof.

key_terms.definition_md: For $1 + \sin A$, the expression $1 - \sin A$; their product is $\cos^2 A$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Ratios from one ratio (2 marks):* third side 1, ratios 1.
- *Evaluate with standard values (2–3 marks):* values 1, substitution 1, answer 1.
- *Prove $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$ and derived identities (3–5 marks):* figure and Pythagoras 1, divisions 1 each, conclusions and angle ranges 1.
- *Prove an identity (2–3 marks):* one mark per correct step with its reason.

**Common mistakes**
1. Reading opposite/adjacent from the wrong angle.
2. Treating $\sin A$ as $\sin \times A$, or $\sin^2 30^\circ$ as $\sin 60^\circ$.
3. Assuming $\sin(A + B) = \sin A + \sin B$.
4. Writing $\tan 90^\circ = 0$ (it is not defined).
5. Working on both sides of an identity at once, or moving terms across "=".
6. $\sqrt{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}$ treated as $\sin A + \cos A$.
7. Using complementary-angle results (not in the 2026–27 syllabus).

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, $AB = 20$ cm and $BC = 21$ cm. Then $\sin A$ equals
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $AC = \sqrt{20^2 + 21^2} = \sqrt{841} = 29$ cm. **Step 2.** $\sin A = \dfrac{\text{side opposite } A}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{21}{29}$. Option (b) is $\cos A$ (adjacent side); option (c) is $\tan A$.

questions.stem_md: If $\cos A = \dfrac{12}{13}$ for an acute angle $A$, then $\tan A$ equals
questions.solution_md: Take adjacent side $12k$ and hypotenuse $13k$. The opposite side is $\sqrt{169k^2 - 144k^2} = 5k$. So $\tan A = \dfrac{5k}{12k} = \dfrac{5}{12}$. Option (d) is $\sin A$; option (a) is $\sec A$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these could be the value of $\sin A$ for an acute angle $A$?
questions.solution_md: $\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so $0 < \sin A < 1$ for an acute angle. Only $0.8$ lies between $0$ and $1$ (e.g. a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle).

questions.stem_md: For an acute angle $A$, $\operatorname{cosec} A \cdot \sin A$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\operatorname{cosec} A = \dfrac{1}{\sin A}$, so the product is $1$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $2\sin 30^\circ + \tan 45^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $2 \times \dfrac12 + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2$. Option (c) forgets to double $\sin 30^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\tan^2 60^\circ - 2\sin^2 45^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$, so $\tan^2 60^\circ = 3$; $\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $2\sin^2 45^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac12 = 1$. Value $= 3 - 1 = 2$. Option (d) forgets the second term.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\dfrac{1 + \tan^2 30^\circ}{1 - \tan^2 30^\circ}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan^2 30^\circ = \dfrac13$. Numerator $1 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac43$, denominator $1 - \dfrac13 = \dfrac23$. Value $= \dfrac43 \div \dfrac23 = 2$. Option (b) is the numerator only.

questions.stem_md: If $\sqrt3 \tan\theta = 1$ and $\theta$ is acute, then $\theta$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} = \tan 30^\circ$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. Option (a) comes from $\tan\theta = \sqrt3$.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is not defined?
questions.solution_md: $\tan 90^\circ = \dfrac{\sin 90^\circ}{\cos 90^\circ} = \dfrac10$, which is not defined. The others are $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ and $\cot 90^\circ = \dfrac01 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: As $A$ increases from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, the value of $\cos A$
questions.solution_md: $\cos 0^\circ = 1$, $\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.87$, $\cos 45^\circ \approx 0.71$, $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac12$, $\cos 90^\circ = 0$: it decreases from $1$ to $0$. Option (c) describes $\sin A$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = 30^\circ$, then $2\sin A\cos A$ equals
questions.solution_md: $2 \times \dfrac12 \times \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. (This equals $\sin 60^\circ$.) Option (a) forgets that $\cos 30^\circ$ has $2$ in the denominator.

questions.stem_md: The value of $6\cos^2\theta + 6\sin^2\theta - 4$ is
questions.solution_md: $6(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) - 4 = 6 \times 1 - 4 = 2$, for every $\theta$.

questions.stem_md: For an acute angle $A$, $\sec^2 A\,(1 - \sin^2 A)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A$, and $\sec^2 A \cdot \cos^2 A = 1$.

questions.stem_md: For an acute angle $\theta$ with $\sin\theta = 0.6$, the value of $\sec\theta$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 0.8$, so $\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{0.8} = \dfrac54$. Option (c) is $\cos\theta$; option (d) is $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$; option (a) is $\tan\theta$.

questions.stem_md: For an acute angle $A$, $(\sec A - \tan A)(\sec A + \tan A)$ equals
questions.solution_md: It is a difference of squares: $\sec^2 A - \tan^2 A = 1$, since $1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A$.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 2$, then $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta$ equals
questions.solution_md: Square: $\tan^2\theta + 2\tan\theta\cot\theta + \cot^2\theta = 4$. Since $\tan\theta\cot\theta = 1$, $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta = 4 - 2 = 2$. (Here $\theta = 45^\circ$.) Option (a) forgets the middle term.

questions.stem_md: A wheelchair ramp at a school in Pune rises $1.5$ m over a horizontal distance of $2$ m. The sine of the angle the ramp makes with the ground is
questions.solution_md: Ramp length $= \sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5$ m. $\sin = \dfrac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.6$. Option (b) is the tangent ($1.5 \div 2$); option (c) is the cosine.

questions.stem_md: For an acute angle $A$, $\tan A$ can be greater than $1$.
questions.solution_md: $\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$, and the opposite side can be the longer leg: $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3 \approx 1.73$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin A = \dfrac35$ in a right triangle, then the side opposite $A$ must be $3$ cm long.
questions.solution_md: $\sin A$ is a **ratio**. It fixes only the shape: the opposite side could be $3$ cm, $6$ cm or $1.5$ cm, with the hypotenuse $5$, $10$ or $2.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: $\cos 0^\circ = 1$. (It is $\sin 0^\circ$ that equals $0$.)

questions.stem_md: $\sin 30^\circ + \sin 60^\circ = \sin 90^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac12 + \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt3}{2} \approx 1.37$, but $\sin 90^\circ = 1$. Sine does not add like that: $\sin(A + B) \ne \sin A + \sin B$ in general.

questions.solution_md: This is $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ rearranged.

questions.solution_md: $\tan A = \dfrac{1}{\cot A} = \dfrac{15}{8}$. Answer: 15/8.

Evaluate $6\tan^2 30^\circ + 4\cos^2 60^\circ - 3\sec^2 45^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\tan^2 30^\circ = \dfrac13$, $\cos^2 60^\circ = \dfrac14$, $\sec^2 45^\circ = 2$. **Step 2.** $6 \times \dfrac13 + 4 \times \dfrac14 - 3 \times 2 = 2 + 1 - 6 = -3$.

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac12 \times \sqrt3 \times \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75$.

questions.stem_md: If $\theta$ is acute and $2\sin\theta - 1 = 0$, find the value of $3\tan^2\theta + 4\cos^2\theta$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\sin\theta = \dfrac12$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$. **Step 2.** $3 \times \dfrac13 + 4 \times \dfrac34 = 1 + 3 = 4$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sec\theta = 1.25$ and $\theta$ is acute, find $\tan\theta$ using an identity.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta - 1 = 1.5625 - 1 = 0.5625$. **Step 2.** $\tan\theta = 0.75$ (positive, as $\theta$ is acute).

questions.stem_md: If $\operatorname{cosec} A = 2.6$ and $A$ is acute, find $\cot A$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $\cot^2 A = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A - 1 = 6.76 - 1 = 5.76$. **Step 2.** $\cot A = 2.4$.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, the hypotenuse $AC = 20$ cm and $\sin A = 0.6$. Find the perimeter of the triangle in cm.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** $BC = AC \sin A = 20 \times 0.6 = 12$ cm, and $AB = \sqrt{400 - 144} = 16$ cm. **Step 2.** Perimeter $= 20 + 12 + 16 = 48$ cm.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin\theta + \cos\theta = 1.4$ for an acute angle $\theta$, find $\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Square: $\sin^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1.96$, so $1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1.96$. **Step 2.** $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{0.96}{2} = 0.48$. (Indeed $\sin\theta = 0.6$, $\cos\theta = 0.8$ or the other way round.)

questions.stem_md: If $A = 45^\circ$, find the value of $\sec^2 A + \operatorname{cosec}^2 A$.
questions.solution_md: $\sec 45^\circ = \operatorname{cosec} 45^\circ = \sqrt2$, so the value is $2 + 2 = 4$.

questions.stem_md: Given $7\tan A = 24$, find $\sin A$ and $\sec A$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\tan A = \dfrac{24}{7}$: take the opposite side $24k$ and the adjacent side $7k$. Hypotenuse $= \sqrt{576k^2 + 49k^2} = 25k$.

$\sin A = \dfrac{24}{25}$ and $\sec A = \dfrac{25}{7}$.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $XYZ$, right-angled at $Y$, $XY = 9$ cm and $YZ = 12$ cm. Find $\sin X$, $\cos X$ and $\tan X$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$XZ = \sqrt{81 + 144} = 15$ cm.

$\sin X = \dfrac{YZ}{XZ} = \dfrac{12}{15} = \dfrac45$, $\cos X = \dfrac{XY}{XZ} = \dfrac{9}{15} = \dfrac35$, $\tan X = \dfrac{YZ}{XY} = \dfrac{12}{9} = \dfrac43$.

questions.solution_md: Identify the side opposite X (YZ) and the side adjacent to X (XY) first.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate $\dfrac{2\cos^2 60^\circ + 3\sec^2 30^\circ - 2\tan^2 45^\circ}{\sin^2 30^\circ + \cos^2 45^\circ}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Numerator: $2 \times \dfrac14 + 3 \times \dfrac43 - 2 \times 1 = \dfrac12 + 4 - 2 = \dfrac52$.

Denominator: $\dfrac14 + \dfrac12 = \dfrac34$.

Value $= \dfrac52 \div \dfrac34 = \dfrac52 \times \dfrac43 = \dfrac{10}{3}$.

questions.solution_md: $\sec 30^\circ = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, so $\sec^2 30^\circ = \dfrac43$.

questions.stem_md: Find the acute angles $A$ and $B$, with $A > B$, if $\tan(A + B) = 1$ and $\sin(A - B) = \dfrac12$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\tan(A + B) = 1 \Rightarrow A + B = 45^\circ$; $\sin(A - B) = \dfrac12 \Rightarrow A - B = 30^\circ$.

Adding: $2A = 75^\circ$, so $A = 37.5^\circ$ and $B = 7.5^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Both $A + B$ and $A - B$ are acute here, so each equation has exactly one solution.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\cot\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{2\cos^2\theta - 1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$ for every acute angle $\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md:
LHS $= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$.

Since $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$, the numerator is $\cos^2\theta - (1 - \cos^2\theta) = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$. So LHS $=$ RHS.

questions.solution_md: Write everything in sine and cosine, then use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

questions.stem_md: If $x = 3\sec\theta$ and $y = 3\tan\theta$, show that $x^2 - y^2 = 9$.

answer.model_answer_md: $x^2 - y^2 = 9\sec^2\theta - 9\tan^2\theta = 9(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta) = 9 \times 1 = 9$.

questions.solution_md: Uses $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, $AB = 5$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. Riya writes $\sin A = \dfrac{5}{13}$. Find her mistake and give the correct value.

answer.model_answer_md:
$AC = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ cm. She used the side **adjacent** to $A$ ($AB$), which gives $\cos A$.

The side opposite $A$ is $BC = 12$ cm, so $\sin A = \dfrac{12}{13}$.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan\theta = \dfrac12$ for an acute angle $\theta$, find $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ using identities.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: If $\tan\theta = \dfrac43$, find the value of $\dfrac{2\sin\theta - \cos\theta}{2\sin\theta + \cos\theta}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take the opposite side $4k$ and the adjacent side $3k$; the hypotenuse is $5k$. So $\sin\theta = \dfrac45$ and $\cos\theta = \dfrac35$.

$\dfrac{2 \times \frac45 - \frac35}{2 \times \frac45 + \frac35} = \dfrac{\frac85 - \frac35}{\frac85 + \frac35} = \dfrac{1}{\frac{11}{5}} = \dfrac{5}{11}$.

questions.stem_md: If $\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \cot\theta = \dfrac13$ for an acute angle $\theta$, find $\operatorname{cosec}\theta + \cot\theta$, and hence find $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ and $\cot\theta$.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: Aman claims that for some acute angle $\theta$, $\sin\theta + \cos\theta = 1.5$. Is he right? Justify.

answer.model_answer_md:
$(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

Since $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \ge 0$, we have $2\sin\theta\cos\theta \le \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$. So $(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 \le 2$, i.e. $\sin\theta + \cos\theta \le \sqrt2 \approx 1.414$.

As $1.5 > 1.414$, Aman is **not** right. (The largest value, $\sqrt2$, occurs at $\theta = 45^\circ$.)

questions.stem_md:
(a) For an acute angle $A$ of triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $B$, prove that $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$.

(b) Hence derive $1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A$, stating the angles for which it holds.

(c) Derive $\cot^2 A + 1 = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A$, stating the angles for which it holds.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By Pythagoras' theorem, $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$. Dividing each term by $AC^2$: $\left(\dfrac{AB}{AC}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{BC}{AC}\right)^2 = 1$, i.e. $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$. (It also holds for $A = 0^\circ$ and $A = 90^\circ$.)

(b) Divide $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$ by $AB^2$: $1 + \left(\dfrac{BC}{AB}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{AC}{AB}\right)^2$, i.e. $1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A$. It holds for $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$ ($\tan$ and $\sec$ are not defined at $90^\circ$).

(c) Divide by $BC^2$: $\left(\dfrac{AB}{BC}\right)^2 + 1 = \left(\dfrac{AC}{BC}\right)^2$, i.e. $\cot^2 A + 1 = \operatorname{cosec}^2 A$. It holds for $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ$ ($\cot$ and $\operatorname{cosec}$ are not defined at $0^\circ$).

A road in Shimla climbs steadily: for a horizontal distance of $120$ m it rises $50$ m.

(a) Find the length of the road along the slope.

(b) Find $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle the road makes with the horizontal.

(c) Is $\theta$ more or less than $30^\circ$? Justify using the values of sine.

(d) If the road were built at exactly $30^\circ$ over the same horizontal $120$ m, how much would it rise? (Use $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\sqrt{120^2 + 50^2} = \sqrt{14400 + 2500} = \sqrt{16900} = 130$ m.

(b) $\sin\theta = \dfrac{50}{130} = \dfrac{5}{13}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{120}{130} = \dfrac{12}{13}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{50}{120} = \dfrac{5}{12}$.

(c) $\sin\theta = \dfrac{5}{13} \approx 0.385$, which is less than $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$. Since $\sin\theta$ increases as $\theta$ increases from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, $\theta < 30^\circ$.

(d) Rise $= 120\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{120}{\sqrt3} = 40\sqrt3 \approx 40 \times 1.732 = 69.28$ m.

questions.solution_md: The real road rises only $50$ m, consistent with $\theta < 30^\circ$.

By (a), $p^2 + q^2 = 1 - 2pq$, so $p^3 + q^3 = 1 - 2pq - pq = 1 - 3\sin^2 A\cos^2 A$.

(c) $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac12$, $\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$: LHS $= \dfrac{1}{64} + \dfrac{27}{64} = \dfrac{28}{64} = \dfrac{7}{16}$. RHS $= 1 - 3 \times \dfrac14 \times \dfrac34 = 1 - \dfrac{9}{16} = \dfrac{7}{16}$ ✓.
